cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Program 7: Caring for Children and Families — Paediatric Nursing

cards.title: Welcome to GNPS Program 7
cards.body: Infants, children and adolescents are not simply smaller adults. Their anatomy, physiology, communication, development and responses to illness differ markedly across age groups.

bullets.label: This programme develops the essential
bullets.text: This programme develops the essential knowledge, assessment skills and professional behaviours required to provide safe, developmentally appropriate and family-centred care — aligned with national nursing education programmes and regulatory bodies worldwide.

bullets.label: Apply nursing principles across infancy, childhood and adolescence
Assess physical growth, developmental milestones and age-specific vital signs
Use age-appropriate communication and validated pain-assessment tools
Provide care for respiratory, cardiac, gastrointestinal and neurological conditions
Calculate and administer medicines safely using weight-based principles
Promote child wellbeing, injury prevention and recognise abuse or neglect

cards.title: WHY THIS MATTERS
cards.body: Children Can Deteriorate Rapidly

bullets.label: Children may not describe symptoms clearly.
bullets.text: Children may not describe symptoms clearly. Early warning signs can be subtle — a change in behaviour, reduced feeding, grunting, lethargy or fewer wet nappies.

bullets.label: Safe paediatric nursing depends on careful observation, developmental knowledge and early action.

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Growth, Development & Family-Centred Care

bullets.label: Development influences how children
bullets.text: Development influences how children communicate, respond to illness and participate in care. Nurses must adapt assessment to developmental stage — and treat families as essential partners.

bullets.label: Reflex-driven; bonding with caregiver; sensory development
Rapid motor growth; emerging language; parallel play
Imaginative play; cause-and-effect thinking; fears of body harm
Logical reasoning; peer relationships; need for explanation
Developmental milestones guide expected
bullets.text: Developmental milestones guide expected progress. Persistent delay or loss of previously acquired skills requires further assessment.

cards.title: Family-Centred Care & Communication
cards.body: Age-Appropriate Language

bullets.label: Use simple words, demonstration and distraction to reduce fear in young children
Use dolls or equipment to explain procedures before they happen
Parents know the child's normal behaviour best — value and involve them in all decisions

cards.title: 📋 Clinical Example: A four-year-old is frightened before a blood test. The nurse uses a doll to demonstrate the procedure, explains in simple language and allows the child to choose which arm to present. The parent remains nearby. Developmentally appropriate preparation reduces fear and improves cooperation.
cards.body: Adapt

bullets.label: Match communication to the child's developmental stage
Offer limited choices to give the child a sense of control
Involve the family in comfort and care throughout

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Paediatric Assessment & Recognition of Deterioration

bullets.label: Children may compensate for serious illness
bullets.text: Children may compensate for serious illness before deteriorating suddenly. Systematic, age-specific assessment and early recognition are essential nursing competencies.

cards.title: A Systematic Approach to Assessment
cards.body: Observe

bullets.label: Appearance, posture, breathing, colour before touching.
Age-specific heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure.
Fontanel, capillary refill, urine output, consciousness.
Observation before examination is a critical
bullets.text: Observation before examination is a critical first step — a quiet, floppy or poorly responsive child may be seriously unwell.

bullets.label: Infants & non-verbal children — face, legs, activity, cry, consolability
Children 3+ — self-report using facial expressions scale
Neonates post-operatively — crying, oxygen, expressions, sleep

cards.title: Red Flags: Recognising Deterioration
cards.body: Airway & Breathing

bullets.label: Stridor, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, poor air entry, central cyanosis
Dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanel, prolonged capillary refill, reduced urine output
Irritability, lethargy, seizures, altered consciousness or poor feeding
📋 Clinical Example: An infant with
bullets.text: 📋 Clinical Example: An infant with bronchiolitis becomes quieter and less interested in feeding. The nurse notes nasal flaring, chest retractions and reduced wet nappies. Deterioration is recognised and urgent review requested.

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions

bullets.label: Safe care combines early recognition,
bullets.text: Safe care combines early recognition, evidence-based intervention and family support across respiratory, cardiac, gastrointestinal, neurological and endocrine conditions.

cards.title: Common Conditions & Priority Nursing Actions
cards.body: Key Red Flags — Escalate Immediately

bullets.label: Bilious (green) vomiting in any infant or child
Non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash with fever
Always escalate these signs without delay. Do not wait for confirmatory tests.

cards.title: 📋 Clinical Example: A school-age child with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing and increasing drowsiness. The nurse checks glucose and ketones, recognises possible diabetic ketoacidosis and activates urgent medical management immediately.
cards.body: Recognise

bullets.label: Know the condition-specific red flags and act on them early
Track breathing, hydration, consciousness and response to treatment
Address the needs of the child and the family throughout acute illness

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Medication Safety, Nutrition & Child Protection

bullets.label: Paediatric medication doses are weight-based —
bullets.text: Paediatric medication doses are weight-based — small errors carry serious risk. Nutrition, hydration and safeguarding are equally central because children depend on adults for their protection.

cards.title: Four Pillars of Safe Paediatric Practice
cards.body: Medication Safety

bullets.label: Confirm weight in kilograms. Check dose,
bullets.text: Confirm weight in kilograms. Check dose, concentration, route and maximum safe dose. Always seek independent verification for high-risk medicines.

bullets.label: Feeding needs change from infancy to
bullets.text: Feeding needs change from infancy to adolescence. Use growth charts, dietary history and feeding observation to identify undernutrition, obesity or difficulty.

bullets.label: Educate families on safe sleep, car restraints,
bullets.text: Educate families on safe sleep, car restraints, drowning, burns and poison storage — tailored to the child's age and developmental stage.

bullets.label: Injuries inconsistent with history, unusual
bullets.text: Injuries inconsistent with history, unusual bruising, fearfulness or delayed presentation may indicate abuse or neglect. Report through approved legal pathways.

cards.title: 📋 Clinical Example: A toddler is prescribed a medicine based on weight. The nurse discovers the recorded weight was entered in pounds rather than kilograms. Administration is paused, the child is reweighed and the dose recalculated. The correction prevents a potentially serious overdose.
cards.body: ✅ Always use kilograms

bullets.label: Never assume — confirm the current weight at every encounter
Independent verification is mandatory for weight-based and high-risk doses
Safeguarding concerns must be documented and escalated without delay

cards.title: Level 1 Complete — Your Foundation is Set
cards.body: By completing GNPS Program 7 — Level 1, you have developed foundational knowledge and skills across four core areas of paediatric nursing.

bullets.label: Assess children across age groups and support families as partners in care
Recognise early warning signs and respond to paediatric emergencies
Deliver safe, evidence-based care for childhood illness
Apply medication safety principles and fulfil safeguarding responsibilities
These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 —
bullets.text: These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse, where the focus expands to complex paediatric care, international standards and advanced safeguarding.

cards.body: Caring for Children and Families

bullets.label: Section 1: Growth, Development and Family-Centred Care
Growth and development shape how children
bullets.text: Growth and development shape how children communicate, respond to illness, understand procedures, and participate in their own care.

bullets.label: Paediatric nurses must adapt every assessment
bullets.text: Paediatric nurses must adapt every assessment and intervention to the child's developmental stage — whilst recognising parents and carers as essential partners in care.

bullets.label: Key motor, language and social markers

cards.title: Growth & Development Across Age Groups
cards.body: Each stage brings distinct physical, cognitive, language and psychosocial needs. Always consider both chronological age and individual ability.

bullets.label: Rapid physical growth; bonding and sensory stimulation are paramount
Motor exploration and language emergence; separation anxiety is common
Imaginative play; magical thinking; fears of bodily harm
Logical thinking; peer influence; needs honest, clear explanations
Identity formation; privacy, autonomy and confidentiality are critical

cards.title: Developmental Milestones
cards.body: Milestones provide expected benchmarks for motor, language, social and cognitive progress. Variation is normal — but two key warning signs must prompt further assessment:

bullets.label: Developmental screening should be embedded in routine nursing assessment, not treated as a one-off event.
Failure to reach expected milestones within an accepted age range
Loss of skills a child had previously acquired — always investigate

cards.title: Communication & Therapeutic Play
cards.body: Simple Language

bullets.label: Use short sentences, concrete words and demonstrate before you do
Play reduces fear, builds trust and helps children process procedures
Limited, safe choices restore a sense of control and reduce distress
Offer privacy, respect and opportunities to speak independently

cards.title: Family-Centred Care
cards.body: Parents and carers are expert witnesses to their child's normal behaviour. Their knowledge is a clinical asset.

bullets.label: Parental concern is clinically significant — listen and document
Share information clearly and include families in care planning
Encourage parents to remain present and provide comfort during procedures

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Putting It Into Practice

bullets.label: A four-year-old is frightened before a blood test.
The nurse uses a doll to demonstrate the
bullets.text: The nurse uses a doll to demonstrate the procedure, explains it in simple language, and allows the child to choose which arm to present. The parent remains nearby for reassurance.

bullets.label: Result: Reduced fear and improved cooperation.

cards.title: NCLEX Connection: Key Principles
cards.body: These concepts are high-yield for internationally qualified nurses preparing for the NCLEX examination.

bullets.label: Match vocabulary, explanation depth and interaction style to the child's age and ability
Use play as a clinical communication tool
Therapeutic play is an evidence-based nursing intervention, not optional enrichment
Persistent delays or skill loss require escalation and multidisciplinary assessment
Treat families as partners in care
Family-centred care is a core competency — not a courtesy

cards.title: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 7 · Level 1 Qualified Nurse

cards.title: Why Paediatric Assessment Is Different
cards.body: Children are not small adults. They compensate remarkably well for illness — then deteriorate suddenly and without warning. This makes early, systematic recognition a critical nursing skill.

bullets.label: Assessment must account for age-specific
bullets.text: Assessment must account for age-specific physiology, developmental stage, and the child's ability to communicate distress.

bullets.label: Early recognition saves lives. The window for intervention is often narrow in paediatric patients.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Perform a structured, head-to-toe paediatric assessment with confidence
Select and apply age-appropriate pain scoring tools accurately
Recognise signs of respiratory distress and dehydration early
Identify early warning signs and escalate without delay

cards.title: Observation First — Before You Touch
cards.body: The most powerful assessment tool is your eyes. Before any physical examination, observe the child from a distance to gather vital information without causing distress.

bullets.label: Alert? Interactive? Floppy or unusually still?
Visible effort? Nasal flaring? Abnormal posture?
Does the child respond normally to the parent or carer?

cards.title: Vital Signs and Pain Assessment
cards.body: Age-Specific Normal Ranges

bullets.label: Heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure
bullets.text: Heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure vary significantly with age. Always compare against age-appropriate reference ranges — adult norms do not apply.

bullets.label: FLACC — Infants and non-verbal children (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability)
Wong-Baker FACES — Children aged 3 and above

cards.title: Airway and Breathing — A Priority Every Time
cards.body: Children have smaller, more vulnerable airways and significantly higher oxygen demands than adults. Any sign of respiratory compromise must be treated as urgent.

bullets.label: High-pitched noise on inspiration — indicates upper airway obstruction
Expiratory grunting suggests alveolar collapse and severe distress
Increased work of breathing — a key early warning sign
Subcostal, intercostal or sternal — indicates significant respiratory effort

cards.title: Hydration and Neurological Status
cards.body: What to Look For

bullets.label: Hydration assessment in children relies on multiple clinical cues together. No single sign is sufficient alone.
A child who is unusually quiet or difficult to rouse is a serious concern.

cards.title: The Systematic Paediatric Assessment Framework
cards.body: Observe

bullets.label: Vital signs, pain score, airway status
A consistent, stepwise approach ensures no
bullets.text: A consistent, stepwise approach ensures no critical findings are missed — even under pressure. Move through each step methodically, escalating at any point if deterioration is identified.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Infant with Bronchiolitis
cards.body: The Scenario

bullets.label: An infant with known bronchiolitis becomes
bullets.text: An infant with known bronchiolitis becomes quieter and less interested in feeding. The nurse notices a change from the child's earlier behaviour.

bullets.label: The combination of behavioural change,
bullets.text: The combination of behavioural change, increased respiratory effort, and reduced urine output indicates deterioration — not simply a quieter phase of illness.

bullets.label: The nurse escalates immediately and requests an
bullets.text: The nurse escalates immediately and requests an urgent medical review. Early escalation prevents a potentially life-threatening event.

bullets.label: Trust your clinical instincts. A child who seems "not quite right" warrants prompt review.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Carry these principles into every paediatric assessment you perform:

bullets.label: Behaviour, colour and breathing from a distance reveal critical information before you approach the child.
Vital sign norms change with age. Adult reference values are not appropriate for children.
Any signs of increased work of breathing require immediate assessment and prompt escalation.
Poor Feeding and Reduced Output Are Red Flags
These subtle cues often precede visible deterioration — never dismiss them as insignificant.

cards.title: Caring for Children and Families: Paediatric Nursing
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 7 · Level 1 Qualified Nurse

bullets.label: SECTION 3: NURSING CARE FOR COMMON CHILDHOOD CONDITIONS

cards.title: Introduction
cards.body: Children frequently require nursing care for a range of conditions affecting the respiratory, cardiac, gastrointestinal, neurological, and endocrine systems.

bullets.label: Safe, effective paediatric nursing combines three core principles:
Include the child and family throughout care

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Outline appropriate nursing care for common childhood illnesses across key body systems
Identify clinical warning signs that require immediate escalation
Track vital signs and clinical indicators to evaluate effectiveness of interventions
Provide holistic, compassionate support during acute illness episodes

cards.title: Respiratory Conditions
cards.body: Conditions such as asthma, bronchiolitis, croup, pneumonia and cystic fibrosis can significantly impair a child's breathing and oxygenation.

bullets.label: Continuously assess work of breathing, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation
Upright positioning and prescribed supplemental oxygen to optimise airway patency
Administer bronchodilators and nebulised medications as prescribed and monitor response
Maintain adequate hydration and monitor closely for signs of respiratory fatigue

cards.title: Cardiac Conditions
cards.body: Congenital heart disease and heart failure in children may present subtly. Nurses must recognise early clinical indicators and adapt care accordingly.

bullets.label: Activity and feeding may need to be paced to reduce cardiac workload.
Poor feeding and failure to gain weight
Respiratory difficulty with reduced activity tolerance

cards.title: Gastrointestinal Conditions
cards.body: Gastroenteritis and dehydration are among the most common presentations in paediatric nursing. Accurate assessment distinguishes routine illness from surgical emergency.

bullets.label: Oral or IV rehydration, monitor fluid balance and output
Assess skin turgor, fontanel, mucous membranes and urine output

cards.title: Neurological & Endocrine Conditions
cards.body: Seizures, meningitis, type 1 diabetes, and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) all require rapid, structured assessment and prompt escalation.

bullets.label: Maintain airway, time the seizure, administer rescue medication as prescribed
Non-blanching rash, bulging fontanel or neck stiffness — escalate immediately
Deep (Kussmaul) breathing, altered consciousness and fruity breath are urgent signs

cards.title: Clinical Example: Recognising DKA
cards.body: CASE STUDY

bullets.label: A school-age child with known type 1 diabetes
bullets.text: A school-age child with known type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, deep (Kussmaul) breathing and increasing drowsiness.

bullets.label: Delayed recognition of DKA can lead to rapid deterioration — act early.
Check blood glucose and ketone levels immediately
Recognise clinical picture as possible diabetic ketoacidosis
Activate urgent medical team and initiate DKA protocol

cards.title: Red-Flag Symptoms: Know When to Escalate
cards.body: Prompt escalation of red-flag symptoms is a professional and ethical responsibility. When in doubt — speak up, escalate early, document clearly.

bullets.label: Memorise warning signs across respiratory, cardiac, GI, neurological and endocrine systems
Continuously assess breathing, hydration status and level of consciousness
Bilious vomiting, non-blanching rash or altered consciousness require immediate action
Effective paediatric care includes compassionate, clear communication with parents and carers
NCLEX Tip: Questions on paediatric conditions
bullets.text: NCLEX Tip: Questions on paediatric conditions often test your ability to prioritise and escalate — practise identifying the single most urgent nursing action.

decks.title: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 7 - Level 1 - Section 4 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Paediatric Nursing: Medication Safety, Nutrition & Child Protection
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 7 · Level 1 · Section 4

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be equipped to deliver safe, evidence-based paediatric care across four critical domains.

bullets.label: Apply weight-based dosing principles accurately and safely
Assess growth, feeding and nutritional status at every stage
Promote age-appropriate safety strategies within family education
Recognise and report signs of abuse or neglect through approved pathways

cards.title: Medication Safety: Getting the Dose Right
cards.body: In paediatric nursing, small errors carry serious consequences. Weight-based dosing requires precision at every step.

bullets.label: Always verify the child's current weight in kg
bullets.text: Always verify the child's current weight in kg before any calculation. Never estimate or rely on recorded values without checking.

bullets.label: Dose, concentration, route, frequency and maximum safe dose must all be verified — even for familiar medicines.
High-risk paediatric medicines require a second
bullets.text: High-risk paediatric medicines require a second qualified nurse to independently check the calculation prior to administration.

cards.title: Clinical Example: A Near-Miss Prevented
cards.body: CASE STUDY

bullets.label: A toddler was prescribed a weight-based
bullets.text: A toddler was prescribed a weight-based medication. The nurse identified that the recorded weight had been entered in pounds rather than kilograms — a critical unit error.

bullets.label: Administration was immediately paused. The
bullets.text: Administration was immediately paused. The child was reweighed, and the dose was correctly recalculated from the verified weight in kilograms.

bullets.label: A potentially serious overdose was prevented through diligent checking — a reminder that verification saves lives.

cards.title: Nutrition & Growth Across Childhood
cards.body: Nutritional needs evolve significantly from infancy through adolescence. Ongoing assessment ensures every child grows and thrives.

bullets.label: Breast milk or formula is the sole nutrition
bullets.text: Breast milk or formula is the sole nutrition source. Monitor feeding frequency, weight gain and latch or bottle tolerance.

bullets.label: Introduction of solid foods and family meals. Watch for fussy eating, iron deficiency and appropriate portion sizes.
Balanced diet supports learning and growth. Screen for undernutrition, obesity and disordered eating early.
Rapid growth demands increased nutrients.
bullets.text: Rapid growth demands increased nutrients. Assess for eating disorders, skipped meals and peer-influenced dietary choices.

cards.title: Assessing Nutrition & Growth
cards.body: Key Assessment Tools

bullets.label: Growth charts: Plot weight, height and BMI against age-appropriate centile lines
Dietary history: Explore meal patterns, variety, portion size and appetite changes
Feeding observation: Directly observe feeding to detect swallowing difficulties or aversion
Hydration markers: Assess skin turgor, mucous membranes, urine output and fontanelle in infants
Identify undernutrition, obesity or feeding difficulty early — they all impact long-term development.

cards.title: Injury Prevention: Tailored to Age & Development
cards.body: Accidents are the leading cause of childhood injury. Nurses play a vital role in educating families on age-specific hazards.

bullets.label: Back position, firm mattress, no loose bedding — reduces sudden infant death risk
Age and weight-appropriate seats, correctly fitted and rear-facing for infants
Constant adult supervision near water; pool fencing; no unsupervised bathing
Medicines, cleaning products and chemicals stored out of reach, in locked cabinets
Hot liquid safety, stove guards, smoke alarms and sun protection tailored to age

cards.title: Safeguarding: Recognising Abuse & Neglect
cards.body: Warning Signs to Recognise

bullets.label: Injuries inconsistent with explanation; unusual bruising patterns; multiple injuries at different healing stages
Fearfulness, withdrawal, regression in development; excessive hunger or fatigue
Poor hygiene, inadequate clothing, delayed presentation for care, failure to thrive
Inconsistent explanations, indifference, hostility, or avoiding healthcare contact
Nurses have a mandatory legal and professional
bullets.text: Nurses have a mandatory legal and professional duty to report safeguarding concerns through approved organisational pathways — never ignore your instinct.

cards.title: The Safeguarding Reporting Pathway
cards.body: Identify

bullets.label: Inform senior nurse or safeguarding lead.
Maintain records and support the child.
Acting promptly and following your
bullets.text: Acting promptly and following your organisation's safeguarding protocol protects the child and ensures the nurse meets all legal obligations under child protection legislation.

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: 🔢 Use Kilograms

bullets.label: Always confirm weight in kg. Unit errors are a leading cause of paediatric medication harm.
Independent verification of high-risk and weight-based doses is non-negotiable.
Use growth charts, dietary history and feeding observation across all developmental stages.
Include age-appropriate injury prevention in every family education opportunity.
Follow approved safeguarding pathways. Early reporting protects children and supports families.
